name: Tris-biphenyl triazine
lead: Tris-biphenyl triazine (TBPT), marketed under the trade name Tinosorb A2B, is a synthetic ultraviolet (UV) filter used in sunscreen and daily-wear skincare products. It belongs to the triazine family of filters, which also includes bemotrizinol (Tinosorb S) and phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine [1][2][3].

Published descriptions present it as a relatively recent addition to the small list of UV filters authorised in Europe, and as a particulate (nanoparticle-type) filter that absorbs UV light and also scatters part of it [4][5]. Wikipedia lists it among UVA- and UVB-protective filters, with approval status and maximum concentrations that differ by jurisdiction [3].

Published work on the filter consists mainly of formulation, optical and photochemical studies, plus its use as a photostabilizer for other filters such as avobenzone [6][7]. No clinical trials of its appearance effects were found. In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed only in passing, as one ingredient in sunscreen formulations.
infobox: Approved in the EU; approval and limits vary by country [3]

paras: A 2015 paper describes tris-biphenyl triazine as a newly launched filter that helps formulators reach high protection and the recommended broad-spectrum criterion of a critical wavelength of at least 370 nm, in a market with relatively few authorised filters [4]. A 2016 review of newer UV absorbers places it alongside other triazine filters developed in recent decades [5].

Photophysical work has examined how its spectra and energy dissipation change from single molecules to nanoparticles [8]. A 2025 study reported that light scattering contributes to the protection provided by nanoparticulate filters, using this compound as the example [9].

A 2021 laboratory study evaluated tris-biphenyl triazine as one of three photostabilizers (alongside ethylhexyl methoxycrylene and a citrate-based stabilizer) for avobenzone combined with retinyl palmitate and octyl methoxycinnamate, assessing photostability and phototoxicity [6]. Analytical methods for measuring avobenzone and tris-biphenyl triazine together in formulations have also been published [7].

Regulatory approval and maximum permitted concentrations vary by jurisdiction [3]. A 2020 review of sunscreen design notes that currently used UV filters in general have limitations that researchers cite, including systemic absorption, endocrine disruption, allergy and cytotoxicity concerns [10]; that review is about filters as a class, not this compound specifically. Environmental risk assessment frameworks have used UV filters as case studies [11].
No studies found. Published research is limited to laboratory, optical and formulation studies [4][6][8][9].

The compound is not a subject of its own community protocols. Skincare discussions that mention it treat it as an ingredient in broad-spectrum sunscreens, where proponents of sun protection for skin-aging prevention may look for newer filters; this reflects general sunscreen discussion rather than claims specific to the compound.

card.note: Approval and permitted concentrations differ by country.

quick.overview:
Tris-biphenyl triazine is a synthetic UV filter sold as Tinosorb A2B. It is a particulate triazine-class filter that absorbs UV and also scatters some light, and it is described as a recent addition to the filters authorised in Europe.

Published work is largely laboratory and formulation research. No clinical trials of its effects on skin appearance were found.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVB and UVA radiation, and published optical work reports that scattering by its nanoparticles contributes to protection. It has also been tested as a photostabilizer for avobenzone.
quick.risks: No compound-specific human safety trials were found. Regulatory approval and maximum concentrations vary by country, and UV filters as a class are the subject of ongoing safety and environmental assessment.
